entities.name: Alonso Tostado
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alonso Tostado, also known as Tostado de Madrigal (c. 1400–1455), was a towering intellectual figure of 15th-century Castile, renowned for his encyclopedic erudition that earned him the moniker 'Doctor Fundatissimus.' A prodigious theologian, philosopher, and exegete, his intellectual prowess deeply influenced the court of King John II of Castile and left an indelible mark on scholastic thought during the transition from the late Middle Ages to the early Renaissance in Spain. His vast literary output, encompassing commentaries on scripture, philosophical treatises, and legal opinions, positioned him as a central arbiter of knowledge in his era.

Tostado's career saw him serve as a royal councillor to John II, where his legal and theological expertise was frequently consulted on matters of state and ecclesiastical policy. He held the prestigious position of professor at the University of Salamanca and briefly served as Bishop of Ávila in 1454, though his tenure was short-lived due to his death the following year. His most significant contributions lie in his voluminous writings, which included an extensive commentary on the Bible (the *Commentaria in Matthaeum* and *Commentaria in Ezechielem*), a defense of the Council of Basel, and numerous works on moral philosophy and canon law. He mastered Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, allowing him to engage directly with original scriptural texts.

His comprehensive theological and philosophical works became standard texts for centuries, particularly within Spanish universities, shaping the intellectual discourse for subsequent generations of scholars and clerics. Tostado's insistence on textual accuracy and his mastery of ancient languages prefigured aspects of Renaissance humanism, even as he remained firmly rooted in scholastic traditions. His meticulous approach to biblical exegesis and his synthesis of diverse knowledge streams provided a foundational resource for the burgeoning intellectual life of the Iberian Peninsula.

His work as a royal councillor also gave him direct impact on the political and ecclesiastical landscape of the Castilian monarchy.
